passage:
Monday. Suraj was helping Pradeep with quadratic equations. "Just do the D thing, then plug into the formula, easy." He raced through three lines, using phrases like "the D thing" and "the usual trick". Pradeep nodded and said "Got it" at every step.

Wednesday. In the class quiz, Pradeep stared at the first question and left half the paper empty. Afterwards he showed Suraj the blank sheet. "I said got it. I didn't."

Saturday. Suraj tried again. What was D? What did a, b and c stand for? He solved one equation slowly and wrote down every step, then handed Pradeep the pen. Pradeep solved the next one with a single mistake, and they fixed it together.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say at every step on Monday?
qa.a: Pradeep said "Got it" at every step.

qa.q: What might Suraj have felt when Pradeep showed the blank quiz sheet?
qa.a: Surprised and guilty, realising the nodding had hidden the confusion.

qa.q: What changed in Suraj's second explanation?
qa.a: Suraj explained what D, a, b and c stood for, solved one equation slowly with every step written down, and handed Pradeep the pen.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep have kept nodding and saying "Got it"?
qa.a: Pradeep probably did not want to seem slow or hold Suraj up, so nodding felt easier than admitting confusion. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping steps and using class shorthand while the friend nods without understanding.

passage: Vasudha, sit. I heard you got cross with your friend today, so let me tell you something about me. I'm Divyansh, your uncle, and at sixteen I was the circuit expert in class. Meera asked me to explain Ohm's law. I said, "V equals I R, just rearrange it, the usual, you know," and scribbled symbols fast. She nodded, and I felt clever. Next day she showed me her notebook: three wrong answers and question marks all over. "I nodded because everyone else gets it," she said quietly. I had skipped every step that felt obvious to me. So I took a torch battery, a bulb and a wire, and let her change one thing at a time. That afternoon she finally said, "Oh!"

qa.q: What did Divyansh say when explaining Ohm's law?
qa.a: Divyansh said, "V equals I R, just rearrange it, the usual, you know."

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after Meera nodded?
qa.a: Clever and satisfied, thinking the explanation had worked.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Divyansh explained?
qa.a: After seeing the question marks in the notebook, Divyansh used a battery, a bulb and a wire so Meera could change one thing at a time.

qa.q: Why did Meera nod even though she did not understand?
qa.a: Meera thought everyone else understood and did not want to be the only one who did not.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he skipped obvious steps with shorthand and a nodding friend did not understand.

passage: In the college learning centre, Mahima, a third-year, sat with junior Vandana over a statistics sheet. Mahima had scored well last year and explained mean and spread easily. Then Vandana asked, "Why do we square the differences?" Mahima opened her mouth and found nothing. She had always just done it. "Give me till tomorrow," she said, and felt her ears go hot. That night she reread the chapter, drew a number line, and tried explaining aloud to the wall. The next day she showed Vandana that squaring stops plus and minus from cancelling out. Vandana wrote it down. "Thanks," Mahima said. "You made me learn it properly."

qa.q: What question did Vandana ask that Mahima could not answer?
qa.a: Vandana asked, "Why do we square the differences?"

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when her ears went hot?
qa.a: Embarrassed, having realised she had only ever done it out of habit.

qa.q: What did Mahima do to fill the gap in her understanding?
qa.a: She reread the chapter, drew a number line, explained aloud to the wall and returned the next day with the reason.

qa.q: How might Vandana have seen Mahima's "Give me till tomorrow"?
qa.a: As honest and trustworthy, since Mahima came back the next day with a real answer.

grounding: Shows a student tutor finding a gap in her own understanding through a junior's question and fixing it.

passage:
Dear Alka,
You once told me the best way to learn something is to teach it, and I laughed. This month I've been tutoring a first-year in programming, and you were right. On Tuesday she asked why a function can call itself without going on forever. I said, "Because of the base case," and she said, "But what is that doing?" I had no answer beyond the words. That night I traced a small example on paper, step by step, then explained it to my flatmate's cat. On Thursday I showed her, and she said, "Oh, it stops at zero!" I now keep a page in my notebook called "Questions I couldn't answer". It is already my most useful page.
Naveen

qa.q: What did the first-year ask on Tuesday?
qa.a: The first-year asked why a function can call itself without going on forever.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when the first-year asked "But what is that doing?"
qa.a: Caught out and uneasy, since Naveen had the words but no real reason behind them.

qa.q: What did Naveen do to close the gap before Thursday?
qa.a: Naveen traced a small example on paper step by step and explained it aloud, then showed the first-year.

qa.q: What might it be like for the first-year to ask a hard question and get a clear answer two days later?
qa.a: Satisfying and encouraging, since the first-year went from confusion to "Oh, it stops at zero!" 🙂

grounding: Shows a student tutor whose learner's questions expose gaps in the tutor's own understanding, driving a clearer explanation.

passage:
"Farida, sorry, where do I click to filter the sheet?"
"I showed you yesterday." Farida sighed and reached for the mouse. "Top row. Data. Filter. It's not hard."
"Okay. And then the sort?"
"Same thing. Honestly."
"Right. Yes. Got it."
Damini nodded at the screen, though the menu had already gone. She did not ask again. In the evening she copied the numbers by hand into a new sheet, which took two hours, and hoped nobody would ask why.
"All good?" Farida called, packing up.
"All good."
On the way home Damini thought: everyone else seems to understand, and she had not wanted to be the slow one.

qa.q: How long did Damini take copying the numbers by hand?
qa.a: Copying the numbers by hand took two hours.

qa.q: Why did Damini say "Got it" when she had not understood?
qa.a: Damini felt slow and embarrassed after Farida's sigh and did not want to be the slow one.

qa.q: What could Damini do next to actually learn the filter?
qa.a: Ask for a short, slow demo when Farida is not in a hurry, or write the steps down and repeat them back.

qa.q: How might Farida see the exchange?
qa.a: Farida probably thinks the task is simple and does not realise the sigh made Damini stop asking, so Farida believes all is good.

grounding: Shows a learner pretending to follow an impatient expert and quietly stopping questions.

passage: Looking back, my first month at the design studio taught me more about teaching than about design. Parveen, the senior who had to show me the software, spoke fast and sighed when I asked anything twice. "Just use the layers, it's obvious." After the third sigh I stopped asking. I nodded, wrote nothing, and stayed late redoing files I had misunderstood. What I remember most is the heat in my face. I was not stupid. I just needed the first step slowly. When Parveen was away for a week, a colleague showed me the same tool in ten minutes without any hurry, and it clicked. It was never the tool. It was the tone. - Madhav

qa.q: What did Parveen say about the layers?
qa.a: Parveen said, "Just use the layers, it's obvious."

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling after the third sigh?
qa.a: Ashamed and slow, with heat in the face, so Madhav stopped asking.

qa.q: What small step could Madhav take with a hurried teacher next time?
qa.a: Ask for the first step to be shown slowly just once, or write the steps down and repeat them back.

qa.q: How might Parveen have seen the situation?
qa.a: Parveen probably thought the software was simple to explain and did not realise the sighing made Madhav stop asking.

grounding: Shows a learner made to feel slow by an impatient expert's tone, who then stops asking questions.

passage: Fifteen minutes before opening, Simran had to show Manjula, the new hire, how to record a returned item in the stock sheet. "What do you do when a customer buys something?" Simran asked. "I subtract one from the sheet," Manjula said. "Good. A return is the opposite." Simran did one example: a red kettle back, plus one. "Now explain it back to me, as if I'm the customer." Manjula frowned, explained, and got the sign wrong. Simran did not sigh. "Try the next return." A blue mug: Manjula added one and typed it correctly. The shutter went up on time, and the first return of the day was Manjula's, done alone.

qa.q: What was the item in Simran's example return?
qa.a: It was a red kettle.

qa.q: What might Simran have wanted when asking Manjula to explain it back?
qa.a: Simran wanted to check that Manjula really understood, not just nodded, and stayed patient despite the ticking clock.

qa.q: What made the explain-back step useful?
qa.a: It showed the sign error early, before a real customer, and gave Manjula a chance to fix it with the next return.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt on getting the sign wrong and not being sighed at?
qa.a: Probably nervous but reassured, able to try again because Simran stayed patient. 🙂

grounding: Shows an explainer starting from what the learner knows, giving one example and asking for it back in the learner's words.

passage: In the office store room, Anand slid a blank delivery form towards Lokesh, the new intern. "Have you ever written a receipt at your uncle's shop?" "Yes, every Sunday." "This is the same, plus one line for who signs." Anand filled one in for a box of files and read it aloud. Lokesh nodded quickly. "Great. Now tell me in your own words what goes where." Lokesh explained it, put the signature line under the date, and stopped. "Try the next one alone," Anand said, handing over two boxes. Lokesh's first form had the address in the wrong box. They fixed it together. By the fourth form Lokesh needed no help.

qa.q: Where had Lokesh written receipts before?
qa.a: Lokesh had written receipts at an uncle's shop every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Anand hope to find out by asking Lokesh to explain in Lokesh's own words?
qa.a: Whether Lokesh had really understood, since a nod alone does not show it.

qa.q: Why was giving a small task better than accepting a quick nod?
qa.a: The wrong box showed up on the first form while Anand was there to fix it, so the mistake was caught in practice and not later.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt about the address in the wrong box?
qa.a: Slightly embarrassed but relieved it was caught during practice with Anand there to help.

grounding: Shows an explainer starting from familiar experience, giving one example, asking for it back and setting a small task to test understanding.

subtype: Parent or elder teaching a skill [Observer]
passage: Note by Chinmay, volunteer at the community workshop. Observed on Tuesday: Rajni was teaching a teenager to change a bicycle tyre. The tyre kept slipping. Rajni's hands twitched twice, and both times Rajni put them behind the back and asked, "What do you think is wrong?" It took the teenager eleven minutes, and fingers were pinched once. Rajni stepped in only when asked, and then showed just one move: lever on the opposite side. Then hands off again. The tyre held. The teenager said, "I did it," and was still grinning when Rajni handed over the pump. I will suggest we do this on more benches. - Chinmay

qa.q: How long did it take the teenager to change the tyre?
qa.a: It took the teenager eleven minutes.

qa.q: What was the teenager feeling at the end, and what shows it?
qa.a: Proud and delighted, shown by saying "I did it" and grinning.

qa.q: What did Rajni do when the teenager finally asked for help?
qa.a: Rajni showed just one move, the lever on the opposite side, and then stepped back again.

qa.q: What might Rajni have been feeling when Rajni's hands twitched twice?
qa.a: An urge to take over the task, along with the restraint to let the teenager struggle a little.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing an elder who lets a young learner struggle before giving one small hint.

subtype: Parent or elder teaching a skill [Observer]
passage: Sunday. Watched Irfan Chacha teach my cousin to hammer a nail properly in the balcony workshop. First nail bent. Second nail bent. My hands itched to say something, and I could tell Chacha's did too, but Chacha kept sipping tea instead. Third nail went in halfway, and my cousin said, "It's the way I hold it." Only then did Chacha say, "Try holding further down." Fourth nail went in straight. My cousin's face! I would have grabbed the hammer by the second nail. Note to self: when I teach, sip the tea. - Dhruv

qa.q: How many nails did the cousin hammer, and which one went in straight?
qa.a: The cousin hammered four nails, and the fourth went in straight.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling while watching the bent nails?
qa.a: Impatient and itching to step in, but impressed by Chacha's patience.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do next time when teaching?
qa.a: Stay quiet and wait for the learner to name the problem, then offer one small hint.

qa.q: Why might Irfan Chacha have waited for the cousin to say "It's the way I hold it"?
qa.a: Chacha let the cousin discover the problem first, so the tip to hold further down would make sense.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing an elder letting a young person struggle a little before stepping in with one hint.

subtype: Group project where parts do not fit [Observer]
passage: In the last week before submission at the small-town college, Binita watched her group join their parts on one dusty laptop. Disha had built the survey table with distances in kilometres; another member had entered the distances in miles; a third had written the report assuming 200 houses when the survey covered 120. The graphs would not load. The three of them stared at each other and at the wall clock. Nobody had checked the pieces together until now. Binita, who had only been asked to proofread, said quietly, "We each did our part. We never agreed the units." They stayed until ten fixing it. On the back of her notebook Binita wrote: agree the format first, join a small piece early.

qa.q: What units did Disha use for distances in the survey table?
qa.a: Disha used kilometres.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling as the parts fail to join?
qa.a: Uneasy and a little helpless, since she was only asked to proofread.

qa.q: What early step would have caught the problem?
qa.a: Agreeing the units and format at the start, and joining a small piece together early as a check.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt on discovering the mismatch?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed or defensive, since the table followed a different assumption that no one had agreed on.

grounding: Shows a student group finding at the end that their parts were built on different assumptions and do not join.

subtype: Group project where parts do not fit [Observer]
passage: The night before the demo, Freya sat on the library floor with her laptop while three teammates tried to connect their pieces. Selin's login screen sent a username, but the database that another teammate had built expected an email address. The third page used a colour theme that made the text vanish. Nobody had run all three together before that night. "I thought it was obvious," Selin said. "It was in my head." In the chat thread, each of them had written "my part is done". Nobody had written what passes between the parts. They stayed until one in the morning, and the demo ran with a shortcut. Freya stuck a note on her monitor: interface first, test together early.

qa.q: What did Selin's login screen send?
qa.a: Selin's login screen sent a username.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling while the teammates tried to connect their pieces?
qa.a: Anxious and helpless, watching the clock without a way to fix it herself.

qa.q: What would have caught the mismatch earlier?
qa.a: Agreeing in writing what passes between the parts at the start and running all the pieces together early.

qa.q: What did Selin mean by "It was in my head"?
qa.a: Selin assumed everyone knew the plan and so never wrote it down, which means the assumption was never shared.

grounding: Shows a group of students discovering the night before a demo that separately built parts do not fit.

passage: I'm Salma, and I sat next to Samir on his last day before moving to another office. Samir spent the final hour typing a handoff for the supplier contract renewal: four lines. "Renewal due end of month. Contact is R. Nair. Prices in the shared file." Samir closed the laptop, smiling. I did not say anything; I was not the one receiving it. But I knew that the last supplier call had gone badly, and that the price in the file was one Samir had agreed verbally. None of that was in the note. Two weeks later the new person phoned the supplier and was quoted a higher price. I wonder if Samir simply thought it was obvious.

qa.q: What did the handoff note say about the contact?
qa.a: The note said the contact is R. Nair.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when closing the laptop, smiling?
qa.a: Relieved and satisfied, believing the four-line note covered everything.

qa.q: What could Samir have added before leaving?
qa.a: The background of the last supplier call, the price agreed verbally and any risks, or a short walkthrough call.

qa.q: How might the new person have felt on being quoted a higher price?
qa.a: Surprised and stuck, with no background to explain the gap, through no fault of their own.

grounding: Shows a worker leaving a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows the background that only lived in memory.

passage:
Friday. Akash was moving to a new team on Monday and wrote a short note for Pema about the annual fair booking: "Stalls booked. Sound system pending. Ask the caretaker." He signed off, glad to be done.

Tuesday. Pema sent three messages: which sound company? What is the caretaker's number? Was a deposit paid? Akash, busy in the new team, replied with one word: "Later."

Next Friday. The sound company had not been paid and cancelled the slot. Pema found the invoice in Akash's old email. Hearing about it, Akash sat quietly. "I knew all that. I just didn't write it down."

qa.q: What did Akash's note say about the sound system?
qa.a: The note said: "Sound system pending."

qa.q: What might Akash have felt when saying "I knew all that. I just didn't write it down"?
qa.a: Regretful and a bit ashamed, realising that what was known in his head had not travelled.

qa.q: What could Akash have done on the Friday before leaving?
qa.a: Write down which sound company, the deposit, the caretaker's number and the deadline, and offer a short call.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt on finding the cancelled slot?
qa.a: Frustrated and stressed, having had to reconstruct facts without background and lost the booking anyway.

grounding: Shows a worker who hands over a task with a brief note, assuming the successor knows the reasons and details.

passage:
Damini: hi Yogesh, sorry to bother you on leave. I've taken over the vendor payments sheet
Yogesh: no worries! what's up
Damini: there's a row marked "hold" with no note. do I pay or not?
Yogesh: oh that one. hold until they send the corrected invoice
Damini: ok. and which is the real final file, "final_v3_new" or the other one?
Yogesh: v3_new. ignore the rest
Damini: also the sheet says "call Mr. Rao" and I don't know who that is or why 😅
Yogesh: Rao is at the bank. he approves transfers above the usual limit, needs a call first
Damini: would have been good to know before I paid one on Monday
Yogesh: oh no, sorry. let's write it all on one page today 🙏

qa.q: What was the row marked "hold" waiting for?
qa.a: It was waiting for the corrected invoice.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling on finding rows and files with no explanation?
qa.a: Confused and a bit anxious, unsure what to pay or whom to call.

qa.q: What small step could Yogesh and Damini take now?
qa.a: Write everything on one page today: the holds, the correct file and Mr. Rao's role.

qa.q: How does Yogesh react on hearing about Monday's payment?
qa.a: Apologetic and concerned, offering to write it all down straight away.

grounding: Shows a colleague inheriting unfinished work with missing context and unknown risks, and having to reconstruct it.

passage: When Irawati was posted to another block, Vidya took over the ledger at the village seed store. Some entries carried only initials. Three farmers were marked "as agreed". A cupboard was locked with no key in sight, and one phone number had no name beside it. Irawati was on a bus with poor signal. Vidya spent two days going door to door asking what had been agreed, guessed wrongly twice, and gave one farmer the wrong quantity. She did not blame Irawati. Instead she started a new page headed "what I know, what I don't" and sent it over. Irawati's answers came back the next evening.

qa.q: How many days did Vidya spend asking around?
qa.a: Vidya spent two days going door to door.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling while rebuilding the ledger?
qa.a: Uncertain and pressed, worried about making more mistakes.

qa.q: What could Vidya do to cut down on guessing?
qa.a: Write a page of what she knows and what she doesn't and send it to Irawati, as she did.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt on getting Vidya's page?
qa.a: Probably regretful about the missing details but glad to help, since Irawati sent answers back the next evening.

grounding: Shows a colleague inheriting half-known work with unclear entries and missing keys, losing time and making mistakes through no fault of her own.

passage: I'm Ojas, and I sat between two teams, so I heard all of it. The sales team said the monthly report was the data team's job. Vinita, from the data team, said her team only supplies the numbers and sales writes the final version. Both sounded right. Each waited for the other. For three weeks the report went out with wrong totals because nobody checked the step between them. When a client complained, each apologised and pointed at the other. Later both managers agreed to name one person to check the gap every month. I remember thinking that the problem was no single person. It was that the gap belonged to nobody.

qa.q: For how long did the report go out with wrong totals?
qa.a: It went out with wrong totals for three weeks.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel about the cause of the problem?
qa.a: Ojas felt troubled but clear-eyed, seeing that no single person was at fault and that the gap between the teams belonged to nobody.

qa.q: What step fixed the problem?
qa.a: Both managers agreed to name one person to check the gap every month.

qa.q: How did Vinita see the data team's job?
qa.a: Vinita saw it as ending at supplying the numbers, and believed sales wrote the final version.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing that when work falls between two teams each assumes it belongs to the other and nobody owns the gap.

passage: I'm Sharmila, and I live on the ground floor of our housing society. For nine days a tap at the edge of the garden dripped and then ran. The gardener told me the tap was the plumber's business since it was a pipe. Keerthana, the plumber, said garden taps were the gardener's job. Both were calm and certain. I asked the secretary, who said it had not been assigned to anyone. Water pooled by the compound wall and the path turned mossy. Only when a resident's shoe skidded on it did the committee put up a warning sign and write one name against the tap.

qa.q: For how many days did the tap drip and run?
qa.a: The tap dripped and ran for nine days.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have felt watching everyone say it was someone else's job?
qa.a: Frustrated and puzzled, since each person sounded certain and yet nobody fixed it.

qa.q: What finally fixed the problem?
qa.a: The committee put up a warning sign and wrote one name against the tap.

qa.q: How did Keerthana see the tap?
qa.a: Keerthana believed garden taps were the gardener's job, not the plumber's.

grounding: Shows observers noticing a job that falls between two roles with each assuming it belongs to the other until one owner is named.

subtype: Written handoff with state, risks and contacts [Response]
passage: I'm Thomas, and I sat in when Kiran handed the scholarship event to the new coordinator. Kiran had written a two-page note with five headings: Done (venue booked, invitations sent to 60 guests); Pending (catering quote, reply expected Thursday); What could go wrong (the hall projector often fails, so bring a cable); Where things are (shared folder, paper receipts in the green tray); Who to ask (the hall manager, number below). Then Kiran booked fifteen minutes and walked the coordinator through it, asking, "Which part is unclear?" The coordinator asked two questions, and Kiran added two lines. I have seen handoffs that end with "it's all in the folder". This one felt respectful.

qa.q: How many guests had invitations been sent to?
qa.a: Invitations had been sent to 60 guests.

qa.q: What did Kiran intend by adding the fifteen-minute call?
qa.a: To confirm that the coordinator understood and to show respect, wanting the handoff to work without guesswork.

qa.q: What would you keep from Kiran's approach?
qa.a: The five headings and the short call afterwards to check understanding and add missing lines.

qa.q: How might the new coordinator have felt after the call?
qa.a: Reassured and confident, with a clear list and a chance to ask two questions.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a written handoff covering done, pending, risks, locations and contacts, confirmed by a short call.

subtype: Written handoff with state, risks and contacts [Response]
passage:
Monday. Before starting leave, Tushar wrote one page for Chetan about the monthly stock order: the finished steps, the open ones, the risks, where the files were, and whom to ask.

Thursday. Tushar booked twenty minutes and walked Chetan through it. Chetan asked, "What if the supplier is late?" Tushar added a line: "Call the depot manager on the second day, number below."

Next Wednesday. The supplier was late. Chetan opened the page, called the depot manager on the second day, and the order arrived by Friday. Tushar, on holiday, got a message: "Your page worked."

qa.q: What line did Tushar add on Thursday?
qa.a: Tushar added: "Call the depot manager on the second day, number below."

qa.q: What might Tushar have intended with the walkthrough?
qa.a: To make sure Chetan really understood the handoff and felt supported, by giving a chance to ask questions.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that made the difference when the supplier was late?
qa.a: Chetan opened the page and called the depot manager on the second day.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt opening the page when the supplier was late?
qa.a: Calm and prepared, since the risk and the number were already written down. 🙂

grounding: Shows a careful person writing done, pending, risks, files and contacts, then walking the receiver through it.
